title: Future Directions and Benefits
subtitle: Two approved gene therapies, and judging emerging biotechnology by need, feasibility and fairness
subject: Biology
syllabusDotPoints: investigate the uses and applications of biotechnology (past, present and future), including: (ACSBL087)
researching future directions of the use of biotechnology
evaluating the potential benefits for society of research using genetic technologies
Outline the method and outcome of 2 selected gene therapies used to reduce the impact of genetic conditions
Discuss the roles of biological knowledge, genetic engineering and bioinformatics techniques used in biotechnology
inquiryQuestion: How do genetic techniques affect Earth's biodiversity?
lessonIntent: Students can outline the method and outcome of two approved gene therapies (Casgevy and Zolgensma) and evaluate future biotechnology realistically using need, feasibility and fairness.
examSkill: Outline a named gene therapy's method and outcome, then separate evidence-based prediction from hype when judging a future biotechnology.

introVoiceover.text: Welcome back to HSC Biology. Today, gene therapy and the future of biotechnology. Let's get into it.

scenes.heading: The first CRISPR medicine
scenes.body: In 2019, Victoria Gray became the first person in the US treated with CRISPR for sickle cell disease. In 2023 that therapy, Casgevy, was approved.
scenes.callout: How do you tell what biotechnology can do now from what it might do eventually?
scenes.caption: CRISPR went from a 2012 paper to an approved sickle cell therapy in 2023, but approval is not the same as access.

voiceover.text: In twenty twelve, Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier showed that a bacterial system called CRISPR could be programmed to cut DNA at almost any chosen site, work that earned them the twenty twenty Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Then in twenty nineteen, a woman from Mississippi named Victoria Gray became the first person in the United States treated with a CRISPR therapy for sickle cell disease. In twenty twenty three, that treatment, called Casgevy, became the first CRISPR medicine approved anywhere in the world. That's genuinely extraordinary. But here's the discipline this lesson is about. An approval for one disease is not a cure for millions, and plenty of proposed applications are still years away from any patient. So today's skill is telling what biotechnology can actually do now, from what it might do eventually.

scenes.heading: The trend is toward precision
scenes.body: Future biotechnology is trending toward more targeted, precise biological control across several emerging areas.

bullets.text: Gene editing: more targeted changes to DNA at a chosen location.
Synthetic biology: design of biological systems for specific purposes.
Precision breeding and disease screening: more efficient and earlier targeting.

scenes.secondary: The common pattern across these areas is precision: making biological intervention more specific and controlled than earlier methods allowed.
scenes.callout: The shared direction is greater targeting.
scenes.caption: Emerging biotechnology shares one pattern: increasing precision.

voiceover.text: Let's map where biotechnology is heading, because there's a clear common thread. Future biotechnology is trending toward more targeted, more precise biological control. Gene editing makes changes to DNA at a specific chosen location, rather than broad, untargeted alteration. Synthetic biology designs or redesigns biological systems for specific purposes. Precision breeding uses genetic knowledge to guide breeding outcomes far more efficiently. And advanced disease screening detects genetic risk earlier and more accurately. What unites all of these is precision, making biological intervention more specific and controlled than older methods ever allowed. So when a question asks about future directions, the shared direction to name is greater targeting.

scenes.heading: The words you need

bullets.text: Gene editing: targeted alteration of a DNA sequence at a chosen location.
Gene therapy: adding, replacing or editing genetic material in a patient's cells to treat a genetic condition.
Somatic change: alters body cells only, so it is not passed to offspring.
Synthetic biology: design or redesign of biological systems for specific purposes.
Feasibility: whether a technology is practical, effective, safe and scalable beyond trials.

scenes.callout: Feasibility is the reality check on every prediction.
scenes.caption: Gene editing, gene therapy, somatic change, synthetic biology, feasibility.

voiceover.text: Let's pin down the vocabulary, five terms. Gene editing is the targeted alteration of a DNA sequence at a chosen location. Gene therapy is where medicine uses tools like that, adding, replacing or editing genetic material in a patient's own cells to treat a genetic condition. A somatic change alters body cells only, so it isn't passed on to the patient's children, and every approved gene therapy today works this way. Synthetic biology is the design or redesign of biological systems for specific purposes. And feasibility, the one that keeps your answers honest, is whether a technology is actually practical, effective, safe, and scalable outside the lab or a small trial. Hold on to feasibility, because it's the reality check you apply to every confident prediction.

scenes.heading: Gene therapy 1: Casgevy for sickle cell disease
scenes.body: Casgevy edits a patient's own blood stem cells outside the body so they make fetal haemoglobin again.

bullets.text: Method: blood stem cells are collected and edited in the lab with CRISPR Cas9.
The edit disables the BCL11A switch, so the cells make fetal haemoglobin again.
Chemotherapy clears the marrow, then the edited cells are infused back.
Outcome: in trials, over 90% of patients had no severe pain crises for at least a year.

scenes.secondary: Sickle cell disease comes from a single base substitution in the beta globin gene. Fetal haemoglobin does not sickle, so switching it back on reduces sickling.
scenes.callout: Edited outside the body, then returned: an ex vivo gene therapy.
scenes.caption: Casgevy: ex vivo CRISPR edit of blood stem cells switches fetal haemoglobin back on.
scenes.recapSeed: Casgevy edits blood stem cells outside the body to restore fetal haemoglobin.

voiceover.text: So let's make this concrete with two gene therapies that are actually approved and in use. The first is Casgevy, for sickle cell disease. Sickle cell comes from a single base substitution in the beta globin gene, which makes adult haemoglobin clump and bend red blood cells into a sickle shape. Here's the method. Doctors collect the patient's own blood stem cells, and in the lab they use CRISPR Cas nine to disable a genetic switch called the B C L eleven A enhancer. That switch normally shuts down fetal haemoglobin after birth, so disabling it lets the cells make fetal haemoglobin again, and fetal haemoglobin doesn't sickle. The patient then has chemotherapy to clear their bone marrow, and the edited cells are infused back to rebuild it. And the outcome, in the trials, more than ninety percent of patients had no severe pain crises for at least a year. Because the editing happens outside the body, this is called an ex vivo therapy.

scenes.heading: Gene therapy 2: Zolgensma for spinal muscular atrophy
scenes.body: Zolgensma adds a working SMN1 gene to a baby's motor neurons using a harmless viral vector.

bullets.text: Cause: faulty SMN1 genes mean motor neurons die, and muscles weaken.
Method: an AAV vector carries a working SMN1 gene, given as one infusion.
Outcome: all 15 infants in the first trial were alive without permanent ventilation at 20 months.

scenes.secondary: In a historical group of untreated infants with the same severe form, only about 8% reached 20 months without permanent ventilation.
scenes.callout: Casgevy edits a gene outside the body; Zolgensma adds a gene inside it.
scenes.caption: Zolgensma: an in vivo AAV vector adds a working SMN1 gene to motor neurons.

voiceover.text: The second is Zolgensma, for spinal muscular atrophy, or S M A. In its most severe form, a baby inherits two faulty copies of a gene called S M N one, so the motor neurons that control the muscles gradually die, and without treatment most of these babies die or need permanent breathing support before the age of two. Zolgensma takes a completely different approach from Casgevy. Instead of editing anything, it adds a working copy of the gene. The S M N one gene is packaged inside a harmless, modified virus called an adeno associated virus, and it's given as a single infusion into the bloodstream, where it reaches the motor neurons. So this is an in vivo therapy, happening inside the body. The outcome was striking. All fifteen infants in the first trial were alive without permanent ventilation at twenty months, compared with about eight percent of untreated infants in a historical group. And notice, both therapies are somatic, so nothing is passed on to the patient's children.

scenes.heading: Benefits across three sectors
scenes.body: Potential benefits span agriculture, medicine and industry, and are strongest when they solve real problems efficiently and fairly.

bullets.text: Agriculture: improved yield or resilience, targeted breeding for resistance or nutrition.
Medicine: earlier disease detection, more targeted treatment, better biological medicines.
Industry: more efficient biological manufacturing and specialised enzymes.

scenes.secondary: The two gene therapies show the medical benefit is already real for some patients. The point is not that biotechnology solves everything, but that greater targeting can improve outcomes when it proves safe and effective.
scenes.callout: Strongest when they address a real need.
scenes.caption: Potential benefits span agriculture, medicine and industry.

voiceover.text: Now zoom back out to the potential benefits, which span three sectors. In agriculture, future biotechnology could improve yield or resilience under environmental stress, and allow more targeted breeding for disease resistance or better nutrition. In medicine, it could enable earlier detection of disease risk and more targeted treatment, and the two gene therapies we just saw show that benefit is already real for some patients. And in industry, it could deliver more efficient biological manufacturing and specialised enzymes. But notice the careful framing. The point is not that biotechnology will solve everything, it's that greater targeting can improve outcomes, if the technology proves effective and safe in real use. Potential benefits are strongest when they address a real need, efficiently and fairly.

scenes.heading: Prediction is not the same as hype
scenes.body: Scientific possibility is not social reality. Real benefit depends on far more than whether a technology works in a lab.

bullets.text: Evidence-based prediction uses cautious language and recognises barriers.
Hype assumes benefit is guaranteed because the technology sounds advanced.
Large-scale benefit needs safety, regulation, cost, access and acceptance.

scenes.secondary: A technology may work under limited research conditions, but public benefit depends on safety, reproducibility, cost, access and public acceptance.
scenes.callout: Advanced-sounding is not the same as proven.
scenes.caption: Evidence-based prediction recognises barriers; hype assumes guaranteed benefit.

voiceover.text: Now the discipline that separates a careful answer from an overclaiming one. Scientific possibility is not the same as social reality. Students often see that something works in principle and assume it will transform society overnight. Evidence based prediction is different. It builds from current trends and demonstrated capability, it uses cautious language like may, could, and has potential to, and it openly recognises the barriers. Hype, by contrast, assumes benefit is guaranteed simply because the technology sounds advanced, and it ignores safety, access, cost, and acceptance. A technology may work beautifully in a trial, but large scale public benefit depends on safety, regulation, cost, access and public acceptance. So advanced sounding is never the same as proven.

scenes.heading: Fix the overclaim
scenes.question: A student writes: 'This future biotechnology will definitely solve the problem.' Identify why this is too strong, then rewrite it as a scientifically responsible evaluation.
scenes.coachNote: An overclaim uses 'will definitely' and ignores barriers. Use cautious, conditional language and name the conditions for success.
steps: The claim is too strong because it treats benefit as guaranteed.
It ignores safety, effectiveness, scale, cost and access.
Replace 'will definitely' with conditional language like 'has potential to'.
State the conditions: it must prove safe, effective, scalable and accessible in real use.
Rewrite: this biotechnology has potential to help if it proves safe, effective, scalable and accessible.
scenes.caption: Replace 'will definitely solve' with cautious, conditional, evidence-based language.

voiceover.text: Let's fix an overclaim. A student writes, this future biotechnology will definitely solve the problem. Why is that too strong? Because it treats the benefit as guaranteed, when nothing about an emerging technology is guaranteed. It completely ignores safety, effectiveness, scale, cost, and access, all the things that decide whether a lab result ever becomes a real public benefit. So how do we fix it? First, swap out the absolute language, replace will definitely with conditional language like has potential to. Second, name the conditions for success explicitly. A scientifically responsible rewrite reads, this biotechnology has potential to help solve the problem, if it proves safe, effective, scalable, and accessible in real world use. Notice the structure, it keeps the optimism but ties it to evidence and conditions. That conditional phrasing is exactly what the markers reward.

scenes.heading: The big traps
scenes.body: Trap 1: assuming a biotechnology that sounds advanced is guaranteed to deliver. Possibility is not proof.
scenes.secondary: Trap 2: thinking CRISPR always edits only the intended target. Guide RNAs can bind partly matching sequences elsewhere, so off-target edits are a real safety concern. Trap 3: confusing an approved therapy with a widely available one. Casgevy and Zolgensma each cost around US$2 million per patient.
scenes.callout: Potential is not the same as guaranteed success.
scenes.caption: Advanced is not guaranteed; CRISPR has off-target risk; approval is not access.

voiceover.text: Three traps that cost marks in future directions questions. Trap one, assuming that a biotechnology which sounds advanced is therefore guaranteed to deliver. Possibility is not proof, and confident language about an unproven technology reads as hype, not analysis. Trap two, thinking that CRISPR always edits only the intended target. It's highly precise, but the guide RNA can sometimes bind to partly matching sequences elsewhere in the genome, so off target edits are a genuine safety concern that needs extensive screening before clinical use. And trap three, confusing an approved therapy with a widely available one. Casgevy and Zolgensma each cost around two million US dollars per patient, and they need specialist hospitals, so approval is not the same as access. Keep those three straight and your evaluations stay grounded.

scenes.heading: Quick check
scenes.question: Compare how Casgevy and Zolgensma change a patient's cells, and explain why neither treatment is passed on to the patient's children.
scenes.pausePrompt: Pause and compare method, cells and heritability.
answerSteps: Casgevy: blood stem cells are removed, edited with CRISPR to disable the BCL11A switch, then returned (ex vivo).
Zolgensma: an AAV vector delivers a working SMN1 gene straight into the body, reaching motor neurons (in vivo).
One edits an existing gene; the other adds a working copy.
Both change somatic cells only; eggs and sperm are untouched.
Answer: different methods, both somatic, so neither change is heritable.
scenes.caption: Casgevy edits ex vivo, Zolgensma adds a gene in vivo; both are somatic, so not heritable.

voiceover.text: Quick check. Compare how Casgevy and Zolgensma change a patient's cells, and explain why neither treatment is passed on to the patient's children. Pause and compare the method, the cells, and heritability. Right. Casgevy removes blood stem cells, edits them with CRISPR to disable the B C L eleven A switch, and returns them, so it's ex vivo. Zolgensma sends a viral vector carrying a working S M N one gene straight into the body, where it reaches the motor neurons, so it's in vivo. The deeper difference is that one edits an existing gene, while the other adds a working copy. And the heritability part, both change somatic cells only. The patient's eggs or sperm are never touched, so neither change can be inherited. Different methods, same limit, both are somatic therapies.

scenes.heading: Lock it in
points: Future biotechnology is trending toward more targeted, precise control.
Casgevy: blood stem cells edited ex vivo with CRISPR to restore fetal haemoglobin.
Zolgensma: an AAV vector adds a working SMN1 gene to motor neurons in vivo.
Both are somatic, effective in trials, but costly, so approval is not access.
Judge a future biotechnology by need, feasibility and fairness; avoid hype.
scenes.finalPrompt: Evaluating an emerging technology? Ask: real need, feasible at scale, fair access?
scenes.caption: Five takeaways: precision trend, two gene therapies, somatic and costly, need, feasibility, fairness.

voiceover.text: Let's lock it in. Five takeaways. First, future biotechnology is trending toward more targeted, more precise biological control. Second, Casgevy treats sickle cell disease by editing blood stem cells outside the body with CRISPR, so they make fetal haemoglobin again. Third, Zolgensma treats spinal muscular atrophy by using a viral vector to add a working S M N one gene to motor neurons, inside the body. Fourth, both are somatic, both worked strikingly in trials, and both are very expensive, so approval is not the same as access. And fifth, judge any future biotechnology by three questions, is there a real need, is it feasible safely and at scale, and is access fair. See you next lesson.
